problem: Single-agent object-goal navigation for inspection does not scale to large environments; coordinating multiple robots requires shared semantic beliefs, task allocation and robustness to limited or failing communication.
motivation: Inspection in industrial, search-and-rescue and domestic settings needs efficient coverage, faster completion and robustness under uncertainty. Multiple robots can achieve this only if they keep consistent semantic understanding across the team despite communication constraints.
key_idea: Extend semantic-guided object inspection (SEEK) to multi-robot teams via a distributed Relational Semantic Network and shared Dynamic Scene Graph, consensus-based belief fusion, and auction-based conflict-free task allocation.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation details can be cited. The abstract claims near-linear scaling up to four agents and graceful degradation under communication failure, which it attributes to semantic-prior-driven exploration combined with consensus belief sharing and auctions.
method: Distributed Relational Semantic Network (RSN): each agent maintains semantic beliefs about object relations and shares them across the team.
Shared Dynamic Scene Graph (DSG): a common scene representation of inspection findings kept consistent across agents.
Collaborative exploration: exploration guided by semantic priors.
Belief fusion: consensus protocols with claimed provable convergence guarantees.
Task allocation: auction-based, conflict-free assignment of inspection targets.
Adaptive communication protocols: handle communication constraints and failures.

setting.backbone: not specified in abstract (extends SEEK semantic-guided inspection with RSN/DSG)

results: Abstract claims significant speedup over single-agent approaches with high success rates, near-linear scaling efficiency up to four agents, and graceful degradation under communication failures. No numbers are given, and the abstract names no baselines beyond 'state-of-the-art multi-agent coordination methods'.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation; real-robot validation is not shown, although the abstract claims practicality for real-world use.
Scaling is demonstrated only up to four agents.
